articles.title: France's Yellow Vest movement calls new protests for October 31st
articles.text:
France's Yellow Vest movement calls new protests for October 31st
Advertisement
Protests
France's Yellow Vest movement calls new protests for October 31st
AFP - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 24 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 24 Oct 2026 13:44 CET
Add a comment
Women kneel or sit on the ground during a rally of the Women's Yellow Vest protest movement. Photo by Bertrand GUAY / AFP.
Add The Local as a preferred source
France's Yellow Vest movement, which has helped organise protests rocking the country, called Saturday for new demonstrations on October 31.
Organisers called for fresh rallies and a sit-in outside parliament and city halls nationwide, condemning the "authoritarian drift" of President Emmanuel Macron and urging citizens to stand up for "public freedoms".
Another day of nationwide protests began in France on Saturday under tight security, a week after riots and looting erupted on the sidelines of massive cost-of-living demonstrations.
Members of the largely rural based Yellow Vest movement were angered and refused to comply when Paris police ordered a late change to the authorised route for a union-organised march Saturday, shifting it to the edge of the capital.
Next Saturday, "we will protest for the freedom to protest, and for all our freedoms," a Yellow Vest coordinator told journalists at Paris's Bastille square, the original departure point for the march.

articles.title: Police fire tear gas as new French demonstrations kick off
articles.text:
Police fire tear gas as new French demonstrations kick off
Advertisement
Protests
Police fire tear gas as new French demonstrations kick off
AFP - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 24 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 24 Oct 2026 12:51 CET
Add a comment
Protesters take part in a demonstration in favor of purchasing power, the protection of public services, and fiscal and social justice, in Strasbourg, eastern France. Photo by ROMÉO BOETZLE / AFP.
Add The Local as a preferred source
French police started firing tear gas at protesters Saturday as they stepped up security in major cities aiming to prevent a repeat of rioting a week ago, on a day of fresh nationwide demonstrations over the high cost of living.
Police on Saturday arrested 135 people and seized a variety of weapons as they deployed for nationwide demonstrations with orders to prevent renewed street violence, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said.
Weapons confiscated included metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons, he said, while adding that, so far, "there has been no major incident".
Police in the southeast city of Lyon fired tear gas to disperse some 150 protesters near the city centre -- where demonstrations had been banned -- when they briefly tried to block a road, an AFP journalist saw.
Elsewhere, authorities and rattled shopkeepers geared up for potential new street violence.
Near Paris's Bastille neighbourhood, a clothing store had removed all its merchandise from shelves ahead of the demonstrations, while a nearby restaurant was boarded up with signs insisting it was "still open". Many other retailers in the capital also had wooden boards covering their windows.
The Louvre and the Musee d'Orsay museums were closed.
Police were seen readying riot gear in zones that bore the brunt of last weekend's clashes and looting.
They were among 70,000 security personnel the interior ministry said were mobilised to counter the "high" threat of violence.
"We will not tolerate any unrest," Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Friday, adding that calls had been circulating on social media calling for violence and looting.
READ ALSO: Protests in France - What to expect on Saturday, October 24th
Advertisement
Protest against far-right party
Adding to tensions, far-right leader Marine Le Pen's National Rally (RN) party was holding a weekend congress in the central city of Orleans to kick off her campaign for elections in six months to choose President Emmanuel Macron's successor.
Thousands of people yelling anti-fascist slogans marched on Saturday against Le Pen, and also against Macron, a pro-business centrist leader. "Macron resign. Le Pen in prison," the crowd yelled.
The violence last weekend and the heightened tensions over this weekend's demonstrations highlighted the febrile atmosphere in France ahead of that vote, which Le Pen is best-placed, according to surveys, to win.
Last weekend saw rioters on the margins of the nationwide demonstrations clash with police, vandalise public buildings and loot hundreds of stores. Some 2,700 people were arrested and the retail sector said shopowners were left with damage and stolen stock totalling hundreds of millions of euros.
Macron attributed the worst of the violence to "ultra-left" groups that he said "want to bring down the republic".
Groups organising Saturday's renewed demonstrations have accused Macron and his government of ignoring widespread public anger over rising costs, and over classroom conditions for students.
Inflation in France, as elsewhere, has been sent surging by the Middle East war, started in February by US President Donald Trump and Israel.
Protests have also been taking place in Italy, Belgium, Spain and Portugal over different issues, yet with some overlap on inflation and education problems. Italy has sent 500 troops to try to quell street violence in Milan.
Advertisement
Boarded-up shops
In Paris, streets on Saturday were unusually quiet, with many shop windows boarded up, and some of the bigger retailers sent messages to customers warning that they were closed for the day.
The capital's police at the last minute ordered a union-organised march in the city be moved from Bastille, in the centre-east, to the more remote eastern Porte d'Italie on the southern rim of the capital.
Unions said they reluctantly would go along with that. But the Yellow Vest movement -- a loosely organised grouping that staged disruptive street protests against Macron eight years ago -- indicated it would not comply.
Macron and his government have sought to draw a line between the legitimate demands of protesters and the looting, burning and ransacking that erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations last Saturday.
Courts have already sent 217 people, half of them first-time offenders, to prison over the events on Saturday, officials said.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
Macron has said authorities would accept only union-led demonstrations and would counter any others they deemed "illegitimate".
Authorities in Marseille had banned all protests but announced Friday that a union-organised demonstration would be allowed on an "exceptional basis".
The restrictions, including outright bans on protests in some cities, have drawn criticism.
Amnesty International denounced what it called "a slide toward authoritarian practice", saying the measures were "jeopardising the right to demonstrate peacefully".
"Police have a responsibility both to ensure that protests can take place peacefully and safely and to protect the public from violent disorder," said Eva Cosse, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch.

articles.title: Inside France: Violence, looting and zombie walks
articles.text:
Inside France: Violence, looting and zombie walks
Advertisement
Inside France
Members only
Inside France: Violence, looting and zombie walks
Emma Pearson - emma.pearson@thelocal.com
Published: 24 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 24 Oct 2026 11:54 CET
Add a comment
Protesters walk next to tear gas and the statue of Marianne in Place de la République, Paris, on Sunday. Photo by Matthieu RONDEL / AFP
Add The Local as a preferred source
From the violence that shook the country on Saturday to the foreign commentators who tried to use it for their own advantage, via the French enthusiasm for 'blood and gore' Halloween events and some extremely cheesy pop, here's what we have been talking about in France this week.
What a week. On Saturday night I shared my Metro home with some young looters, on Sunday morning I crunched through the broken glass in République and by Monday I was simmering with rage at the ill-informed commentary of those outside France who sought to blame immigration for the violence that swept the country over the weekend.
The 'let's blame the immigrants' game is always tedious, but in this case it's especially ignorant - what, France had no history of violent protest before immigration increased in the post-war period? Did the immigrants use a time machine to storm the Bastille, take to the barricades of the Paris Commune or topple the July Monarchy?
Advertisement
France has its problems, for sure, but they are homegrown French problems.
In fact, I would say that Saturday's violence is actually two problems; on the margins of the peaceful demos, the casseurs turned up to smash, burn and fight with police. Taking advantage of the disorder, many largely apolitical teens and young adults from the banlieues turned up to begin looting.
Without the political violence, the looting would not have happened, but France still needs to address why so many young people - many of them of immigrant origin but born and raised in France as second-, third or even fourth-generation immigrants - are so disengaged that they regard violent social disorder as merely an excuse to go shopping without the inconvenience of paying.
But the violence itself stems from the casseurs, and they are a) French and b) not a new phenomenon. They have been an annoying feature of protests throughout my time in France, and they are very recognisable; young, mostly white and well equipped - hoods to hide their faces, masks and goggles to protect against tear gas and backpacks full of tools and kit to set fires. These are not protesters who get a bit carried away; their intention is to cause trouble, and they are experienced in the cat-and-mouse games with the riot police.
READ ALSO: ANALYSIS: Who are France's 'casseurs' and why can't police stop their violence?
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
They do, however, seem to be getting both more numerous and more extreme. It's notable that on Saturday violence not only flared in the 'usual suspect' towns (Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Nantes) but also in smaller towns including Limoges, where the town hall was burned down. There don't seem to be any simple explanations for why more people feel motivated to get involved in this kind of activity.
A man has been arrested over the Limoges fire - a 34-year-old local man who was already on a watchlist for violence at extreme left and environmental protests. According to French media, his 70-year-old father has also recently been convicted of violent protest and is apparently a believer in one of the maddest conspiracy theories on the internet - namely that the Linky electricity meters are being used by the government to spy on us.
For now, we wait to see what will happen this weekend . . .
Advertisement
Talking France
We discuss Saturday's violence in the latest episode of the Talking France podcast, as well as what we can expect over the next few weeks, and the weighty issue of French debt. But we also managed to lighten the mood a bit with a discussion of our favourite French food festivals and a lively debate on espelette pepper. Listen here.
Fright night
Growing up in the UK in the 1980s, Halloween was not really a thing (we celebrated Mischief Night instead, which is basically 'all trick, no treat') and annual rituals of kids demanding sugar and adults decorating their homes are very much an American import. It's taken root in the UK now, though, especially among the younger generation, and is arriving in France too.
Although it's not as big a thing here, you will certainly see Halloween decorations and merchandise in shops, and some small ghosts and demons walking the streets on October 31st.
One aspect of Halloween that the French have embraced with enthusiasm is the blood and gore - 'zombie walks' full of adults in horrifying costumes are becoming more and more popular.
This remains a big divide between British and American Halloween - in the UK your costume must above all be scary, in order to frighten away the souls of the dead who return on the night of the year when the veil thins between the living and the dead. I mean, it's just basic science. This is the Halloween hill I will die on, clutching a foam rubber hand and a pint of fake blood.
READ ALSO: How do the French celebrate Halloween?
Advertisement
French discothèque
And because this has been quite an intense week, maybe we should finish with some music. I asked my French colleague Emma Albright to create a playlist of the songs that you really need to know to fit in on a French dance floor.
Let's be very clear - these are not the coolest French songs. In fact, they're mostly defiantly uncool but somehow get played at every French wedding, birthday or village fête, and entice every drunk French uncle onto the dance floor. Enjoy!
Inside France is editor Emma Pearson's weekly look at some of the news, talking points and gossip in France that you might not have heard about. It’s published each Saturday and members can receive it directly to their inb

articles.title: French word of the day: Fiché S
articles.text:
French word of the day: Fiché S
Advertisement
French Word of the Day
Members only
French word of the day: Fiché S
The Local France - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 23 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 24 Oct 2026 09:31 CET
Add a comment
Photo: Annie Spratt/Unsplash/ Nicolas Raymond
Add The Local as a preferred source
A piece of police jargon that has made its way into everyday conversation.
Why do I need to know fiché S?
Because you're likely to see this piece of official police jargon in a lot of news headlines, as well as hear it in everyday conversation, at present.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
What does it mean?
In France, a fiche S is part of a national database called the Fichier des Personnes Recherchées (FPR), which is a database of wanted criminals or people on watchlists that was created in 1969.
This database also contains details of escaped prisoners (letter V), people who have escaped from institutions (AL) or people barred from entering the country (IT).
The letter S stands for 'state security' and there are different types of fiches S, with numbers going from S1 to S16 so when someone is described as fiché S, it means that they are suspected of being a threat to state security.
Fiche S is, however, not in itself a cause for arrest.
Around 70 percent of fichés S are made by the French interior security general direction (DGSI), which is the national intelligence service.
Advertisement
You will most commonly hear the term in relation to terrorists, such as when French police raided the homes of dozens of fichés S after the terror attack in Conflans in which a teacher was beheaded.
However, not all fichés S are terrorists - football hooligans can be fichés S. It is the same for some radical environmental activists, or people who have been involved in violent far-left or far-right activism.
A fiche S is kept for two years in the Fichier des Personnes Recherchées and is destroyed if the person has kept a low profile. Otherwise, the fiche S is renewed.
Fiche S refers to the file, while fiché S is the person who is the subject of the file.
Although it's obviously a serious subject, the term has become so ubiquitous in everyday life that some people even use it as a joke.
So for example, if you declare a particularly controversial opinion - a salade Niçoise is actually better with potatoes in it, let's say - your friend might say Ooooh, tu es fiché S ! -  You're on the watchlist now!
Or as in the tweet below "Damn, I don't like cassoulet - that's me going on the watchlist."
Punaise. J aime pas le cassoulet. Je le digère mal. Je vais être fiché S
— hayetbt (@hayetbt) October 21, 2020
Advertisement
Use it like this
Le terroriste arrêté est fiché S depuis quelques années - The arrested terrorist had been on a watchlist for several years.
Elle a été fichée S parce qu’elle participait au blocage de Notre-Dame-des-Landes - She has been recorded as a national security threat because she took part in the blockade at Notre-Dame-des-Landes.
Tu manges des légumes avec ta raclette ? Attention, tu seras bientôt fiché S ! La raclette ne se mange qu'avec des patates et de la charcuterie ! - Do you put veggies with your raclette? Careful, you'll soon be registered as a national security threat! Raclette should only be eaten with potatoes and charcuterie!

articles.title: Lawmakers say EU must probe social media role in protests
articles.text:
Lawmakers say EU must probe social media role in protests
Advertisement
Protests
Lawmakers say EU must probe social media role in protests
AFP - news@thelocal.com
Published: 24 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 24 Oct 2026 09:50 CET
Add a comment
A protester runs during a demonstration against the "high cost of living", in Paris on October 17. Photo by Kiran RIDLEY / AFP.
Add The Local as a preferred source
The EU must urgently investigate the role of social media during protests in member states including France, European lawmakers demanded Friday, adding that Brussels should be prepared to block access "as a last resort".
Hundreds of thousands of high school and university students have rallied in France, Italy, Spain, Belgium and other European countries in recent weeks, with some protests descending into violence.
More than 30 members of the European Parliament (MEPs) co-signed a letter from EU lawmaker Stephanie Yon-Courtin to the bloc's tech chief Henna Virkkunen, calling on Brussels use its digital content rules to get answers from platforms.
READ ALSO: Protests in France - What to expect on Saturday, October 24th
Advertisement
"These events have raised serious questions about the role that social media may have played, whether through calls to gather, the livestreaming of incidents or the circulation of images through recommender systems, as well as about any revenue such content may have generated," they said.
The MEPs from across the political spectrum urged the EU to demand data about the spread of illegal content and what role the algorithms played.
They also want to EU to activate "crisis" mechanisms under the Digital Services Act (DSA) that give Brussels the power for "targeted and proportionate measures".
This could include suspending services as a last resort, they added.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
The EU executive should also boost efforts to protect minors, "who are the most exposed to this kind of contagion", the lawmakers warned.
The European Commission only confirmed it had received the letter, but earlier on Friday, spokesman Thomas Regnier said national authorities had the power under the DSA to seek information themselves from platforms.
"The commission is ready to support and to also play its role if there is a systemic dimension," Regnier said.

articles.title: Reminder - clocks go back in France this weekend
articles.text:
Reminder - clocks go back in France this weekend
Advertisement
Health
Reminder - clocks go back in France this weekend
James Harrington - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 25 Mar, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 24 Oct 2026 08:00 CET
Add a comment
The clocks go forward an hour at the weekend. (Photo by Jeff PACHOUD / AFP)
Add The Local as a preferred source
It's soon time to move into winter time . . .
On the weekend of March 28th and 29th France - together with the whole of the European Union (plus the UK) - moved into summer time.
But summer is now over so it's time for the clocks to go back.
France will move to l'heure d'hiver (winter time) at 3am on Sunday, October 25th. The clocks will move back one hour to become 2am - with the effect the country can enjoy an extra lie-in on Sunday morning.
Advertisement
In recent years, repeated efforts have been made to end the twice-yearly dash round the house changing the time on alarm clocks, cookers, and microwave ovens — but while EU member states now agree that the hour change should be scrapped, finding agreement on which time zone to stick with has proved more difficult.
READ ALSO: 'It's pointless' - Why the French want to end the changing of the clocks
These days, however, most electronic devices — such as smartphones, computers, and televisions — update automatically.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
But, it’s argued the time change can ‘temporarily disrupt your biological clock’, particularly in the October switch back to ‘winter hours’.
The French government’s website recommends “anticipating” the time change by “gradually adjusting your rhythm a few days beforehand”.
In 2019, the French National Assembly organised an online survey on whether French people were in favour of ending time changes. Out of two million responses, some 83.7 percent said they were in favour of ending daylight saving time, while more than 60 percent said they had “negative or very negative experience(s)” with the change.

articles.title: A69: France's newest motorway (finally) set to open
articles.text:
A69: France's newest motorway (finally) set to open
Advertisement
Travel news
Members only
A69: France's newest motorway (finally) set to open
James Harrington - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 19 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 24 Oct 2026 08:00 CET
Add a comment
Employees work on the A69 motorway construction between Toulouse and Castres. (Photo by Matthieu RONDEL / AFP)
Add The Local as a preferred source
France's newest - and most controversial - motorway is due to finally open in south-west France. From the tolls to the route to why it's taken so long, here's what you need to know.
Where is it?
The new two-lane 62km autoroute connects the city of Toulouse, in south-west France, to the Tarn town of Castres – which will lose its tag as the largest town in the country without a direct motorway connection when the A69 finally opens.
Up to now anyone wanting to drive between the two conurbations has had to use the mostly one-lane RN 126.
Driving between Castres and Toulouse using the current route (dark blue) and the new A69 (pale blue). Map: Google Maps
The new road is expected to reduce the journey time between the two towns by between 25 and 35 minutes, depending on the traffic and the time of day.
Long-term plans
This is a very long-term project - the road, expected to open on Friday, November 6th - was first imagined back in the 1990s.
Advertisement
Plans gathered pace after the short dualled A680 opened connecting the RN126 to the A68, which connects Toulouse and Albi, but then stalled again due to strong opposition to the project from environmental groups.
Environmental protests
Climate activist Greta Thunberg took part in a protest against the building of the motorway in February 2024.
Her presence raised the profile of a protest site outside Castres that has beeb the scene of a number of violent clashes during the years-long argument over the road.
The A69 has faced numerous challenges in the courts, all of which were struck down, though construction was halted for several months after one court cancelled important environmental permits.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
The challenges continued even as construction was well underway, and at one point it appeared that the almost-finished road might not be able to open - in the end, however, all challenges were struck down and the completed section is now ready to open.
There will be no toll booths
The A69 will be one of just a handful of so-called ‘free-flow’ toll-paying motorways in France – and the first in the Occitanie region.
That means no toll booths, and therefore no queues to join or get off the motorway. Instead, cameras placed on toll gantries at key points on the route will record vehicle licence plate numbers as they pass, which will in turn allow operator Atosca to calculate how much is owed in tolls.
Drivers will then have to logon to the website later and pay their tolls or - for regular users - register for an account so that payment is automatically taken.

So how much will it cost to use?
That depends on how far you want to travel along it, how often you use it and how environmentally friendly your vehicle is.
For a driver using only part of the motorway, the tolls are as follows:
€1.80 between Castres and Soual Est
€1.90 between Soual Est and Puylaurens
€2.80 between Puylaurens and Maurens-Scopont
€2 between Maurens-Scopont and Verfeil
When travelling the full length of the motorway, including the €1.70 toll for the A68 section, the cost of a one-way trip between Castres and Toulouse is €10.20.
However, tolls will vary depending on the vehicle category. For the entire journey between Castres and Verfeil, motorbike users will pay €5.10 each way. The fare will reach €12.90 for certain vans, motorhomes, and vehicles with high trailers, and €19.10 for Class 3 heavy goods vehicles.
On the other hand, low-emission vehicles benefit from a 20 percent reduction. For a class 1 electric or hydrogen car, a complete one-way journey will cost €6.80. Regular users, meanwhile, will be able to access other discounts.

articles.title: The essential guide to voting from abroad as a US citizen
articles.text:
The essential guide to voting from abroad as a US citizen
Presented by FVAP
The essential guide to voting from abroad as a US citizen
With the US midterm elections fast approaching, it's important for Americans living overseas to make sure they're prepared. We explain exactly how to vote from abroad.
Published: Fri 21 Aug 2026 09:04 CEST
It's easy to register and vote as an American abroad. Image by Eva Michálková from Pixabay
While many Americans abroad are enjoying the summer, election deadlines can approach quickly. Have you made sure you're ready to vote?
An increasing number of Americans living overseas are choosing to make their voices heard at the ballot box.
Approximately 3.3 million US citizens live abroad, with 2.2 million of voting age, and there is a well-established system in place to help ensure their votes are counted.
Over the decades, a simple, secure and effective process has been developed to enable Americans overseas to vote, whether they are serving in the military, working, studying or enjoying retirement abroad.
There are a few key steps Americans outside the United States should take throughout the year to make sure they remain eligible to vote and receive their ballots on time.
Along with the Federal Voting Assistance Program (FVAP), we've outlined the steps you need to follow to make your voice heard in upcoming elections. And with the midterm elections approaching on November 3rd 2026, it's a good time to register so you can take part.
Request your absentee ballot using FVAP's FPCA tool and help ensure that your vote counts
Step one: Make sure you've requested your absentee ballot
You can't vote without a ballot, so the first step is making sure one can be sent to you.
Most Americans abroad do this by completing the Federal Post Card Application (FPCA), which allows election officials to confirm your eligibility and send your ballot to your overseas address or preferred delivery method.
Using the online tool, you'll be asked for your voting residence address and a few other personal details that your local election office can use to identify you.
If you're unsure of your voting residence, FVAP provides guidance to help determine the correct address.
Once you've completed the form, print, sign and submit it according to your state's requirements.
Even if you've voted from overseas before, FVAP recommends submitting a new FPCA each calendar year to ensure your information remains current and your ballot request is active for each election year.
If you're concerned about whether your application has been received, you can contact your local election office directly.
Find important deadlines and ballot-request information on the Federal Voting Assistance Program website
Step two: Complete and return your ballot promptly
After your FPCA has been processed, your absentee ballot will be sent to you using the delivery method you selected, typically email or postal mail.
Once you receive it, complete and return it as soon as possible. Sending your ballot early helps avoid any unexpected delays and ensures it arrives in time to be counted.
Ballot return deadlines vary by state, and each state has its own rules regarding postmarks and receipt dates. FVAP's website provides up-to-date information for every state and territory.
If you're voting from overseas, it's also worth considering local postal delivery times and any seasonal delays that could affect international mail.
Step three: Have a backup plan
International mail is generally reliable – but delays can happen.
That's why FVAP recommends becoming familiar with the Federal Write-In Absentee Ballot (FWAB), a backup ballot available to eligible US citizens living overseas.
If you're concerned that your regular absentee ballot may not arrive or be returned in time, you can complete and submit a FWAB instead.
The FWAB can be completed online or downloaded as a printable PDF and emailed to your election office.
Remember that election officials will only count one ballot. If both your FWAB and regular absentee ballot are received, state rules determine which ballot will be counted.
Step four: Remind family and friends
Life overseas can be busy, and election deadlines can easily slip people's minds.
If you've already requested your ballot and made a plan to vote, take a moment to remind other Americans abroad to do the same.
A quick message to friends, family members or colleagues could help ensure that they have time to register, request a ballot and return it before their state's deadline.
Do you have questions about voting from abroad? Need help requesting a ballot or understanding the process? Visit the Federal Voting Assistance Program website for the latest guidance and resources.
